title: NASA Discovers First Binary Star System Where Both Stars Exploded as Supernovae
excerpt: Using 16 years of Fermi telescope data, Stanford-led researchers identified two supernova remnants in the constellation Gemini as long-separated stellar siblings.
body:
• Scientists have found the first known example of a binary star system where both massive stars exploded as supernovae, leaving behind two detectable remnants — the Jellyfish Nebula and a fainter neighbor called G189.6+3.3.
  • The discovery, published in Nature Communications, used 16 years of NASA Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope data to detect hidden gamma-ray emissions from the overlooked second remnant.
  • Both remnants sit about 6,000 light-years from Earth in the constellation Gemini, with their explosion centers separated by roughly 40 light-years.
  • Computer simulations of a million binary systems support the conclusion, with the probability of a random alignment estimated at less than 1%.

Two massive stars that once orbited each other in a cosmic partnership both met violent ends in supernova explosions tens of thousands of years apart, scientists reported Tuesday in a study published in Nature Communications. The discovery, led by Stanford University, marks the first time astronomers have identified a binary star system in which both companions blew up and left behind observable remnants.

A Hidden Remnant in the Jellyfish Nebula's Shadow

The breakthrough came from 16 years of observations by NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. Researchers detected gamma-ray emissions from a faint supernova remnant called G189.6+3.3, which had been hiding in the glare of its far brighter neighbor, the Jellyfish Nebula (IC 443) — one of the most luminous gamma-ray-emitting remnants in the Milky Way.

https://x.com/NASA/status/2079655118165705100

Both remnants are located about 6,000 light-years from Earth in the constellation Gemini. X-ray evidence suggests that hot plasma from G189.6+3.3 may extend across the entire region, meaning the two remnants overlap almost completely.

"There are so many striking connections between the two remnants that we conclude they're likely related, giving us the first known example of a binary system where both stars have undergone supernova explosions."

— Miltiadis Michailidis, Stanford University

A Millions-Year-Old Story

The two stars were once gravitationally bound in a close binary system, orbiting each other at a distance of just a few multiples of the gap between Earth and the sun. One star was roughly 15 to 25 times more massive than the sun; the other at least 20 times the sun's mass. Both were tens of thousands of times more luminous than our star during their lifetimes.

The star that formed G189.6+3.3 blew up first, between 20,000 and 110,000 years ago, according to the study. The explosion disrupted the binary and sent its companion hurtling through space. After traveling at least 40 light-years, that surviving star also detonated, producing the Jellyfish Nebula roughly 8,000 to 9,000 years ago. Both explosions likely left behind neutron stars.

A bright filament of interstellar gas lies between the two remnants. Observations show the shock wave from G189.6+3.3 slammed into dense gas there and dramatically slowed — key evidence that both remnants interact with the same cloud system, according to co-author Marianne Lemoine-Goumard of the University of Bordeaux.

Backed by a Million Simulations

The researchers ran computer simulations of one million massive binary systems. The models showed that stars orbiting close enough to exchange matter can produce dual supernova explosions with separations and time delays matching those observed. The probability of the observed alignment occurring by chance was less than 1%, according to NASA.

"This system provides a rare opportunity to reconstruct the complete evolutionary history of a massive binary — from the birth and interaction of two massive stars, through both supernova explosions, to the remnants they left behind."

— Miltiadis Michailidis, Stanford University

Why It Matters

Although most massive stars are born in binary systems, no pair in which both have exploded and left behind observable remnants had previously been identified. The discovery gives astrophysicists their first direct test case for theories about how massive stars evolve differently with a close companion — one of the major open questions in stellar physics.

The Jellyfish Nebula is also a candidate "PeVatron," a cosmic particle accelerator capable of boosting protons to extreme energies. Finding a second accelerator nearby could help scientists understand how supernova remnants develop into these rare cosmic engines.

What Comes Next

The team plans further observations to refine the ages and energies of both remnants. Whether the first explosion directly triggered the second remains open — by the time the first star blew up, its companion may already have been nearing the end of its life, according to Michailidis. Future studies could also clarify the velocity "kicks" supernova blasts impart to nearby objects, a process that shapes the broader structure of the galaxy.
